title: Ex-Meta AI Director Rohit Patel Launches Ndoc to Take On Office and Google Workspace
excerpt: After eight years at Meta, most recently as a director at Meta Superintelligence Labs, Patel is building an AI-native workspace that unifies documents, data and presentations — and plans to open-source its file format so users are never locked in.
body:
• Rohit Patel has left Meta after eight years, most recently as a director at Meta Superintelligence Labs, to launch Ndoc, an AI-native alternative to Microsoft Office and Google Workspace.
  • Ndoc unifies work now scattered across Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit and ChatGPT copy-paste into one workspace colleagues can open without an account.
  • The product has three parts: Stage for presentations and dashboards, Narrative for analysis with citations, and Model for the underlying datasets and Python scripts.
  • Patel plans to open-source the ".ndoc.html" file format so documents open in any browser and users are not locked in.

After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company to launch Ndoc, a startup pitched as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office and Google Workspace, TechCrunch reported. Patel, a former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs, is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta, following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan, AI researcher Andrew Tulloch, and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith.

One Workspace Instead of Six Tools

Patel designed Ndoc to be more than another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit and "ChatGPT copy-paste" with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they are not signed up for Ndoc, according to TechCrunch.

https://x.com/AiForAmericans/status/2115145339132928204

The product brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live — slide decks, dashboards, simulations or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures and the "why" behind the numbers. The Model tab houses the underlying datasets and Python scripts.

Built to Be Checked

The design reflects Patel's background. At Meta he focused on reinforcement learning and on evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. His premise for Ndoc is that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work — users can find the Python scripts used to create a document and inspect the data and reasoning behind it, rather than receiving an AI-generated answer on faith.

To avoid the lock-in of the incumbents he is challenging, Patel intends to open-source the ".ndoc.html" file format, allowing documents to be viewed in any web browser and other developers to build compatible applications, as Up Headlines reported.

The Bet

Ndoc is a three-person startup taking on two of the most entrenched product suites in business software. Its wager is that rebuilding the document around AI from the ground up — with verifiable workings attached — beats bolting AI assistants onto files designed decades ago. Whether enterprises will move decision documents off Office and Workspace for that promise is the test ahead.

Ndoc is starting small — a three-person startup — against incumbents whose suites are bundled into nearly every corporate IT contract. Patel's pitch, as reported, is aimed first at the analysis workflow: the spreadsheet, the chart, the deck and the explanation that usually live in four different applications. By keeping the model, the narrative and the presentation in a single file that renders in a browser, the company hopes the unit of work itself, not any single app, becomes the thing teams share.
